contributions.headingText:
In 2019, the International Academy of Cytology (IAC) initiated a process that brought together an international group of cytopathologists to begin the development of a system for standardized reporting of lymph nodes and related organs by fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) cytopathology. The five-category Sydney System for reporting lymph node cytopathology was proposed and published {32454496}. The editors and authors of the WHO Reporting System for Lymph Node, Spleen, and Thymus Cytopathology (WHO System) acknowledge the authors of the Sydney System and the role they have played in the development of reporting FNAB of lymph nodes.

The WHO System is a product of the joint project of the IAC, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), and the WHO, which is producing standardized cytopathology reporting systems across organ systems. This WHO System closely corresponds to the fifth edition of the WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours (WHO-HAEM5), which forms a basis for the diagnosis and treatment of lymphoid lesions, including infectious and inflammatory entities and benign and malignant neoplasms [[WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Haematolymphoid tumours. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2024. (WHO classification of tumours series, 5th ed.; vol. 11). https://publications.iarc.who.int/637.]]. Many of the disease entities that affect lymph nodes, thymus, and spleen have unique FNAB diagnostic cytopathological criteria that are not presented in WHO-HAEM5. The WHO System text presents these key diagnostic criteria, as well as the application of ancillary testing based on FNAB material, within a system of hierarchical categories with cross reference to WHO-HAEM5. This will facilitate the real-world practice of cytopathology of these sites.

The WHO System is a reporting system to assist cytopathologists to assess FNAB of lymph nodes, spleen, and thymus and reflects a cytopathologist’s approach to the material on direct smears. It covers the full range of lesions, including reactive, infectious, metastatic, and haematolymphoid entities found in these sites that can be assessed by FNAB. In regard to the classification of haematolymphoid lesions and entities, the WHO System is based on WHO-HAEM5, which is the key reference as to the terminology and classification of lymphomas. The WHO System includes summaries of the clinical, imaging, and histopathological findings of each lesion in lymph nodes, spleen, and thymus to help a cytopathologist make a diagnosis, and it refers readers to WHO-HAEM5 for further details.

But there are significant differences in the aims and presentation between WHO-HAEM5 and the WHO System. In the WHO System, the lesions and entities affecting lymph nodes, spleen, and thymus are divided between “Benign” and “Malignant” chapters, and there are indeterminate “Atypical” and “Suspicious for malignancy” categories. Many of the entities presented in WHO-HAEM5 are not presented in the WHO System, because FNAB has no role in their diagnosis – most obviously the leukaemias diagnosed on peripheral blood and bone marrow aspirates and related ancillary testing. Other neoplasms have not been reported in the cytopathology literature or are new WHO-HAEM5 entities, while others are difficult to diagnose or cannot be diagnosed on FNAB and are not presented in separate sections but are discussed in the differential diagnosis of more common FNAB entities with a similar cell type and cytopathological features.

The presentation of lesions and entities is based on the cell type or types present. In the “Malignant” chapter, the presentation of lymphomas is based on seven cell types and patterns: mixed lymphoid, predominantly small/intermediate, predominantly intermediate/pleomorphic/blastic, single very large atypical cell pattern, histiocytic/dendritic cell neoplasms, stroma-derived neoplasms of lymphoid tissue, and metastases. Neoplasms of the spleen and thymus are also addressed.

Within each cell type pattern, the lesions or entities most commonly diagnosed by FNAB are presented, matching the cytopathologist’s approach. There is a focus on each entity’s cytomorphological differential diagnosis from other entities with a similar cell type, including any distinguishing cytomorphological clues, and then ancillary testing is presented in detail; for example, most large B-cell lymphomas with a similar “predominantly intermediate/large/pleomorphic/blastic cell pattern” are presented together, because their cytomorphology is similar and their specific diagnosis is based largely on ancillary testing, while two large B-cell lymphomas – lymphomatoid granulomatosis and T-cell/histiocyte–rich large B-cell lymphoma – are placed in the “Single very large atypical cell pattern” grouping, because that is how their cell type and cytomorphology present to the cytopathologist.

The WHO System uses the same definitions as presented in WHO-HAEM5 [[WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Haematolymphoid tumours. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2024. (WHO classification of tumours series, 5th ed.; vol. 11). https://publications.iarc.who.int/637.]] in almost all cases, but there are exceptions; for example, the WHO System definition of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma does not include the peripheral blood requirement, because the WHO System refers to FNAB of lymph nodes. As another example, the WHO System definition of lymphoblastic lymphoma encompasses both T-cell and B-cell lymphoblastic lymphomas, because these cannot be distinguished on cytopathology, but the text following the definition clearly describes both lymphoma types and their distinction on ancillary testing.

The aim of the WHO System is to promote the use of standardized nomenclature in lymph node cytopathology reporting. The diagnostic categories and specific diagnoses are linked to diagnostic management algorithms that assist clinicians in managing patients and improving patient care in all clinical and socioeconomic settings {37702127}. The WHO System provides detailed information on the role and use of FNAB, the techniques of biopsy and specimen preparation to maximize diagnostic potential, and the key diagnostic cytopathological features of each entity. The emphasis is on the cytopathological differential diagnosis to facilitate the use of the system globally, but information on current best practice in the use and reporting of ancillary testing is also provided. Each category has a clear definition and terminology, is associated with a ROM derived from the literature, and is linked to recommendations for further diagnostic workup and management to assist the referring clinician. Standardized report components are recommended, and sample reports are provided for each category. Ultimately, the aim is to raise the profile and promote the use of FNAB cytopathology by increasing awareness of its current diagnostic role in lymph nodes, thymus, and spleen, as well as its potential role in the era of personalized medicine through immunocytochemistry and molecular pathology of small biopsies {37702127}.

Cytopathologists have increasingly demonstrated expertise not only in the diagnosis of infectious and inflammatory processes and metastatic malignancy in lymph nodes, but also in the diagnosis of lymphoproliferative disorders by the use of cytopathological evaluation of FNAB slides and the application of state-of-the art diagnostic and ancillary techniques on FNAB material. In the majority of cases, a diagnosis can be made based on cytomorphology, but infectious and metastatic lesions often require further diagnostic workup. In addition, there are cases where a precise diagnosis of a lymphoma and subtyping is more difficult, and in this setting, FNAB provides excellent material for ancillary tests, particularly when ROSE is used for triage. The ancillary testing includes immunophenotyping by multiparameter flow cytometry, as well as immunocytochemistry on cell blocks (and to a lesser extent on cytospins and direct smears) and molecular studies such as FISH, PCR, and NGS {7395814; 34004059}. This also applies to FNAB of the thymus and spleen. However, while FNAB is a widely used and accepted, accurate diagnostic procedure to diagnose specific infections, such as tuberculous lymphadenitis, and metastatic carcinoma, its role in diagnosing lymphomas is more controversial. This is accentuated by the increasing number of new lymphoma subtypes being described, many of which are defined by features determined only by flow cytometry, immunocytochemistry, and NGS [[WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Haematolymphoid tumours. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2024. (WHO classification of tumours series, 5th ed.; vol. 11). https://publications.iarc.who.int/637.]].

A specific diagnosis of lymphoma by FNAB, therefore, requires a multiparameter approach facilitated by ROSE to obtain sufficient cells for flow cytometry and/or immunocytochemistry, FISH, and NGS. In addition, cell block preparations from needle rinses may be obtained and used to supplement FNAB diagnosis by providing tissue for immune biomarkers. FNAB provides excellent single cells for flow cytometry and particularly well-preserved intact cells for biomarkers and both DNA and RNA NGS studies. The quality of this material can surpass that of DNA and RNA derived from cells obtained by extraction from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue biopsies {16329118}. In experienced hands, this multiparameter approach has demonstrated that the diagnosis of the majority of lymphoid lesions assessed by FNAB can be made with a level of accuracy similar to that obtained by traditional haematopathology. However, it is recognized that some lymphomas do require CNB or surgical excision biopsy with ancillary testing for their diagnosis, such as those with a high percentage of reactive lymphoid cells or T-cell lymphomas. Lymphomas such as Hodgkin lymphoma; T-cell/histiocyte–rich large B-cell lymphoma; nodal T follicular helper cell lymphoma, angioimmunoblastic type; and peripheral T-cell lymphoma therefore require CNB or preferably excision biopsy.

The extent to which the diagnosis of a specific lymphoma subtype is possible depends on the local medical infrastructure and support, as well as the type of practice. For example, a community practice may have far fewer resources for ancillary testing compared with a major oncology hospital. However, although sophisticated immune-profiling and molecular studies may not be available in low- and middle-income countries, cytopathologists in these countries can routinely and effectively diagnose reactive processes, specific infections, metastases, and benign or malignant lesions in lymph nodes and related organs based on cytopathology alone, leaving only a relatively small number of lymphoid lesions where the diagnosis of malignancy is difficult or not possible, for which CNB (if available) or excision biopsy is required. The use of FNAB can greatly reduce the load on hospitals, surgical departments, and histopathology laboratories by selecting the cases that will require surgical excision for histopathology and ancillary testing to make specific lymphoma diagnoses.

The WHO System aims to improve the diagnostic accuracy of FNAB in all these situations, while highlighting the limitations and defining which cases require surgical excision pathology {11601134; 33175094}. The use of the indeterminate diagnostic categories “Atypical” and “Suspicious for malignancy” allows for individual cases to be initially categorized based on their cytopathological findings, and then appropriate ancillary tests can be used to further refine the diagnoses. When this is not possible, excisional biopsy can be recommended.

Although the goal of all FNAB cytopathology is to make a specific diagnosis, in an individual case the cytopathologist must make a risk assessment for that particular clinical situation and categorize a case based on the cytopathological findings and ancillary tests, with or without a specific diagnosis. If there is no clinical or imaging information and no ancillary testing available, the FNAB of a lymph node may be less accurate.

In this first edition of the WHO System, the aim has been to correlate closely with WHO-HAEM5, and changes in this latest edition are mentioned and discussed. Obviously not all processes and tumours presented in WHO-HAEM5 [[WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Haematolymphoid tumours. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2024. (WHO classification of tumours series, 5th ed.; vol. 11). https://publications.iarc.who.int/637.]] are discussed in the WHO System, which specifically presents a reporting system for FNAB cytopathology–assessed lesions. Lymphoproliferative disorders are described based on a review of the evidence in the published literature. A consensus as to key diagnostic criteria has been established by expert cytopathologists with a focus on those entities that have already been recognized as diagnosable with FNAB. Although the text generally follows WHO-HAEM5, the presentation of lesions and neoplasms reflects the cytopathologist’s approach of assessing smear pattern and cell size, as well as cell type recognition.

In response to real-world practice and future research critiquing this WHO System, there will be further refinement of the key diagnostic cytopathology features, ancillary testing, and the risk or rate of malignancy associated with each category, which it is anticipated will be reflected in future editions of this WHO Reporting System for Lymph Node, Spleen, and Thymus Cytopathology.
